stem: A client with chronic heart failure asks what an appropriate nutrition plan generally emphasizes. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Use an overall heart-healthy eating pattern, reduce sodium according to the individualized plan, and follow any fluid limit specifically recommended by the health care team.
options.B: Use one fixed low-sodium and fluid-restriction prescription for every client with heart failure regardless of congestion, laboratory findings, comorbidities, or treatment plan.
options.C: Focus only on total calories because food quality, sodium intake, and individualized fluid guidance have little relevance to heart-failure self-care.
options.D: Increase processed and restaurant foods because they are generally lower in sodium than minimally processed foods prepared without added salt.

rationale: Current American Heart Association guidance recommends an overall heart-healthy dietary pattern that emphasizes vegetables and fruits, whole grains, healthy protein sources, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, and reduced sodium. Heart-failure self-care guidance also addresses sodium reduction and states that some clients may be advised to limit fluid intake, with the daily amount determined by the health care team. The AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline notes that evidence for specific universal sodium and fluid restrictions in heart failure is limited, so these measures should not be converted into one fixed prescription for every client. Therefore, A is correct. B overgeneralizes restrictions, C ignores established nutrition/self-care domains, and D reverses current sodium-reduction guidance.
educational_objective: Teach heart-failure nutrition as an individualized plan built around a heart-healthy dietary pattern, sodium reduction, and fluid guidance when specifically indicated rather than a universal fixed restriction for every client.
source_organization: American Heart Association; American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America
source_document_title: 2026 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health; Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
source_version_date: AHA dietary guidance updated 2026-03-31; HF lifestyle guidance current 2026; HF guideline 2022-04-01
source_locator: AHA 2026 Dietary Guidance → Top Things to Know item 7: heart-healthy pattern emphasizes vegetables/fruits, whole grains, healthy proteins, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, reduced added sugars and sodium. AHA 'Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure' → 'Track your daily fluid intake': some people with HF may be advised to limit fluid and should ask the health care professional how much to drink; 'Eat for a healthy heart' describes the overall heart-healthy pattern. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline → Sections 7.1.1-7.1.2 and 8.2: HF self-care includes sodium restriction, but specific sodium thresholds and routine fluid restriction are supported by limited/low-quality evidence and should not be universalized.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports a heart-healthy dietary pattern with sodium reduction and individualized fluid guidance, while explicitly avoiding a universal fluid or sodium prescription for all heart-failure clients.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort → Nutrition and Oral Hydration: assess nutritional/hydration needs, implement special diets or fluid modifications based on diagnosis and client needs, and provide nutrition-related teaching.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized nutrition and fluid education in chronic heart failure
correction_summary: Rebuilt the broad source item with current 2026 AHA dietary guidance and preserved the important guideline limitation that neither a fixed sodium threshold nor routine fluid restriction should be treated as universal for all HF clients. The final key uses an overall heart-healthy pattern plus individualized sodium/fluid guidance instead of a one-size-fits-all diet.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Nutrition and fluid education in chronic heart failure
audit_findings.source_authority: Current 2026 AHA dietary scientific statement plus official AHA HF self-care guidance and the primary AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline.
audit_findings.currentness: The AHA dietary statement was updated March 31, 2026; current HF lifestyle guidance remains active and the 2022 HF guideline remains the dedicated management guideline.

claim_by_claim.stem: A general nutrition-plan question is appropriate provided the answer avoids a universal HF diet prescription.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because it combines current heart-healthy pattern guidance, sodium reduction, and individualized fluid recommendations.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because the HF guideline does not support one identical sodium/fluid restriction for every client.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because sodium, food quality, and hydration/fluid management are established HF self-care domains.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because packaged, prepared, and restaurant foods are major sodium sources and AHA recommends lower-sodium/minimally processed choices.
claim_by_claim.rationale: No universal sodium milligram target, fluid volume, calorie target, or disease-stage-specific restriction is invented.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to individualized HF dietary teaching.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B tests one-size-fits-all restriction, C calorie-only reductionism, and D reverses sodium-source guidance. Each is clinically plausible and distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A respects both current dietary recommendations and HF-specific individualization. No second option is defensible.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe comprehensive nutrition approaches rather than isolated foods; the key requires understanding individualization rather than grammar.
audit_findings.blueprint: Basic Care and Comfort is directly appropriate because the construct is nutrition and oral-hydration management for an established chronic disease.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether the phrase 'reduce sodium according to the individualized plan' is too vague. It is intentionally nonnumeric because the 2022 HF guideline documents uncertainty about the optimal HF-specific threshold, while 2026 AHA dietary guidance clearly supports lower sodium as part of heart-healthy eating. No unresolved conflict remains.
